Le 11 novembre, j’étais au Carlton Signa: On November 11, I was at the Carlton Signature for the first edition of the Interventum gala, an event launched by the Coalition Pozé to recognize youth workers.
Entre les éclats de rire, les applaudiss: Amid the laughter, the applause and eyes shining with fatigue, you could feel a community that doesn’t give up, despite everything.
Avec quatre jeunes de l’École Converse:: Together with four young people from École Converse, Malika, Abigail Melissa and Razan, we listened to these women and men talk about vocation, exhaustion, solidarity and, above all, the reality facing Montréal’s most vulnerable young people. Their words shaped this article.
Et pour être transparent : la directrice: And in the interest of transparency: the director of La Converse received an award at this event. That said, she had no part in choosing the angle, the approach or the writing of this article.
<strong>Ils travaillent dans l’ombre, so: They work in the shadows, often alone, sometimes unpaid, to prevent violence and rebuild social bonds with Montréal’s most vulnerable young people. On Tuesday, November 11, the Coalition Pozé brought them together for the first edition of the Interventum gala, an unprecedented evening of recognition attended by dozens of youth workers from every corner of the city.
<strong>Une soirée pour ceux qui permett: An evening for those who help young people get through hard times
Saint-Léonard, un soir de tempête. La ne: Saint-Léonard, on a stormy night. Snow piles up on the sidewalks, but inside the Carlton Signature, human warmth wins out. In this building on Langelier Boulevard, nearly 90 people have gathered to celebrate a profession that is rarely in the spotlight: youth work.
By 6 p.m., the lobby is starting to fill. There are hugs, laughter, souvenir photos. Among the guests are inspiring figures, including Guedwig Bernier, former leader of Projet Montréal, pop singer Annabel Oreste, who is also a mental health ambassador for young people, and stars of the profession such as Beverley Jacques, co-organizer of the event and founder of DOD Basketball in Saint-Léonard.
« C’est la première fois qu’on reconnaît: “This is the first time anyone has specifically recognized the frontline workers who work with the most vulnerable young people, the ones people are afraid of, the ones many would rather avoid,” says Pierreson Vaval, executive director of the Coalition Pozé, the organization behind the initiative. These workers, day after day, “agree to put themselves in a precarious situation to go where nobody else wants to go,” Vaval insists.
Il est vrai qu’« on ne fait pas ce trava: It is true that “we don’t do this work to win awards, we do it because it’s a vocation,” says Mohamed Mimoun, director of the Forum Jeunesse de Saint-Michel, who was recognized in the Vocation category. But “it’s important that these people finally get a taste of the recognition they deserve.”
Vingt prix ont été remis ce soir-là, pou: Twenty awards were handed out that night to some thirty people selected for recognition: men and women who work in the alleyways, gyms and youth centres of Montréal-Nord, Rivière-des-Prairies, Saint-Michel, Côte-des-Neiges and Petite-Bourgogne, among other neighbourhoods.
Dans la salle, l’ambiance est celle des: In the room, the mood is that of a big family gathering: familiar faces, reunions, a mix of exhausted and proud laughter.
« C’est la première fois qu’on se voit t: “This is the first time we’ve all seen each other together, the first time we’re celebrating ourselves,” says Karim Coppry, chair of the board of the Coalition Pozé and director of the organization Philo-Boxe, which combines philosophy and boxing to reach young people. “It’s important to recognize those who have been at it for 30 years, as well as those who are just starting out.”
En effet, les organisateurs d’Interventu: Indeed, the organizers of Interventum wanted to bring together youth workers of every generation: the pioneers who carried community work on their backs in the 1990s and 2000s, and the new wave arriving with its own codes and its own language. “We need youth workers that young people can see themselves in, who understand their reality, who come from the same neighbourhoods as they do,” Coppry continues.
<strong>Rendre justice à une vocation d’: Doing justice to a calling of commitment
Harry Delva, intervenant à Saint-MichelP: Harry Delva, youth worker in Saint-Michel. Photo: Jordan Sully
Pour plusieurs des lauréats, cette recon: For many of the winners, this kind of recognition is a first. Taking the stage to receive his Pioneer award, Harry Delva says it is the first time he has been honoured for his work with young people. The surprise is palpable in the audience, which knows this Saint-Michel figure well, active in street outreach for more than 30 years.
Animateur à la radio communautaire, anci: A community radio host and former prevention officer in schools, Harry Delva belongs to that generation of youth workers who turn up in the memories of many young people who are now adults.
« Je me balade dans les rues, autour des: “I walk around the streets, around the schools,” he says. “I talk to the kids, I listen to them, I guide them.” His secret? “Putting yourself in their shoes. Understanding what they’re going through. Because often, they already have the solution. You just have to give them confidence.”
Il raconte aussi que, parmi les jeunes a: He also says that some of the young people he has worked with have become youth workers, managers or entrepreneurs themselves, which he describes as his greatest reward.
Parmi les lauréats, Jordana Larochelle r: Among the winners, Jordana Larochelle receives the Vocation award. A psychosocial worker for more than 12 years, she works with young people placed by the DPJ, Quebec’s youth protection agency, and also coaches basketball for teenagers in Anjou and Pointe-aux-Trembles.
« Pour moi, vocation, c’est un appel, di: “For me, a vocation is a calling,” she says. “It’s not about money. It’s something that lives inside you. You give of yourself because you love it, because it gives you a sense of worth.” She describes how, in group homes, she saw young people who just needed a space and an adult who believed in them. What does she find hardest? “Making others understand how much young people need a place of their own, and youth workers too, and mentors in their lives, so they can become young adults.” Another example: finding a room for basketball practice becomes a fight. “It’s as if,” she continues, “people forget over time that they were young once. They forget that at that age, you need a place, a mentor, an adult who stays.”
Pour Jordanna Larochelle, la reconnaissa: For Jordanna Larochelle, recognition is also about representation: “I think it’s wonderful that so many men are being honoured tonight. In many families, there’s a lack of male figures. These men, these youth workers, become role models.”
La Coalition Pozé, fondée en 2021 dans l: The Coalition Pozé, founded in 2021 in the wake of a series of shootings in Montréal-Nord, began as a citizens’ movement. Its members, frontline workers, wanted to counter violence by giving young people spaces for expression, sport and speaking out.
Quatre ans plus tard, Pozé est devenu un: Four years later, Pozé has become a central part of Montréal’s community fabric.
« Notre approche, c’est le maintien des: “Our approach is to keep young people’s resources in their own environment,” explains Pierreson Vaval. “Young people need significant adults around them, people who can work where most cannot go.”
<strong>L’art comme levier de transmissi: Art as a lever for transmission and healing
Le gala fait aussi une place à l’art, co: The gala also makes room for art, seen as a lever for transmission and healing. Singer-performer Annabel Oreste took the stage to sing, but above all to express her gratitude for this profession. “The first person who made me realize I wasn’t doing well was my youth worker at school,” she tells La Converse. “It’s thanks to her that I understood the environment I was living in was toxic and that there was another world out there.”
Sa voix tremble un peu quand elle ajoute: Her voice shakes a little when she adds: “She saved my life. She was the only one who saw my wound.” Today, <l1>Annabel Oreste puts her story at the service of young people</l1>. “I want them to know that asking for help takes courage. And accepting it takes twice as much.”
Dans les discours de la soirée, un même: In the evening’s speeches, the same observation came up again and again: a glaring lack of resources in the face of exploding needs.
« Il n’y a pas assez d’intervenants à Mo: “There aren’t enough youth workers in Montréal,” says Karim Coppry. “And above all, not enough youth workers that young people can identify with.”
Au-delà des célébrations, Pozé tire la s: Beyond the celebrations, Pozé has been sounding the alarm for several years about <l1>the disinvestment in frontline organizations and the overload of community staff</l1>. “In all the consultations we’ve held with youth workers, the finding is the same: young people are finding it harder and harder to get help in their immediate surroundings,” explains Pierreson Vaval. In his view, this shortage reduces prevention and increases tensions in certain neighbourhoods. As a result, “we need more youth workers in Montréal, Laval and Longueuil,” he says.
De son côté, la Coalition veut soutenir: For its part, the Coalition wants to support frontline workers so that they are better equipped and resources are pooled, he says. “We need,” he says, “to connect them so they can share their experiences, develop joint de-escalation strategies and help calm tensions between groups of young people.”
Malgré les défis, le directeur général r: Despite the challenges, the executive director came away from the gala with renewed conviction, proud of having brought all these people together and feeling that he had met an important need, he says.
Pour Pozé, cette première édition d’Inte: For Pozé, this first edition of Interventum suggests it won’t be the last. “We started somewhere, and we started strong,” says Pierreson Vaval, for whom the evening rekindled the flame of commitment. Some of the young people invited to the evening, in fact, stayed until the very end, captivated by the testimonies. “They felt something that speaks to them,” says the executive director. “Maybe some of them will decide to get involved as youth workers themselves.”
La soirée s’achève sur une ovation. Sur: The evening ends with an ovation. On stage, the winners put their arms around one another’s shoulders, smiling, moved. The trophies are simple, but the symbol is immense: recognition that comes from the field, from peers.
